profiles.name: Albert Rasimavicius
profiles.description:
Albert Rasimavicius was born 1899 in Vabalninkas, Russia (present-day Lithuania). Immigrated to the United States in 1911.

Worked as a coal miner from 1913 to 1918 and then attended Valparaiso University. A member of both the United Mine Workers and the Valparaiso branch of the Communist Party, he was arrested January 10, 1920, when a large quantity of revolutionary literature was found in his room. Deported to Russia March 18, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Alex Targony
profiles.description:
Alex Targony was born 1896 in Volhynia region, Russia. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Born 1896, Volhynia region, Russia. Polish. Driver. Migrated to US 1913. Worked as driver for a milk delivery company in Youngstown, Ohio. Political affiliation unknown, but in 1917 he claimed exemption on his draft registration card on the grounds that he would “not fight against brother.” Arrested sometime prior to January 9, 1920. Deported to Russia, January 22, 1921. No further information found.

Included on list of deported radicals in INS file 54325/36G

profiles.name: Alicia Rosenbaum
profiles.description: Alicia Rosenbaum was a twenty-one-year-old stenographer. Alicia Rosenbaum was arrested with W. E. Spear and Ed Burns in the April 22, 1920 police Red Squad raid on the IWW office in Seattle's Globe Building. A contemporary Swedish-language newspaper identified her explicitly as "Alicia Rosenbaum, alias Alice Rose"; the IWW's own later reporting used Alicia Rosenbaum. The defendants were held for investigation and called toward trial in June 1920. Spear's case was dismissed in January 1921, but no verdict or dismissal notice specifically naming Rosenbaum has been found, so her disposition is unresolved. A 1924 IWW notice identified "Alice Lloyd, also known as Alicia Rosenbaum" — evidence of a further alias, not proof of marriage or a legal name change. Her reported age puts her birth about 1898 or 1899, which is not independently verified, so no birthdate is recorded.

profiles.name: Dionisiy Ivanovich Koval
profiles.description:
Dionisiy Ivanovich Koval was born 1884 in Lutsk Raion, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer.

Joined the Union of Russian Workers in New York in 1919 and escaped arrest during the Palmer Raids on the Russian People’s House in November of that year. He relocated to Waterbury, Connecticut, where he joined the Union of Russian Citizens (an umbrella organization for Russian progressives). Arrested in March 1920, he was deported on January 22, 1921. His wife and two children remained in Russia.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Dmytro Iwankiw
profiles.description:
Dmytro Iwankiw was born 1884 in Stańkowa, Russia (present-day Poland). Worked as a salesman, journalist, steelworker, labor spy. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

May have joined the Union of Russian Workers in 1917 (he denied this after first attesting to it). Recruited in June 1919 by the Armesworthy and Cavitt Detective Agency on behalf of the Youngstown Sheet & Tool Company to inform on Russian radicals. Joined the Socialist Party and then cofounded East Youngstown Ukrainian Branch No. 32 of the Communist Party, serving as its financial secretary, while reporting to company detectives and federal authorities. Arrested during the November 1919 Palmer Raids but released once his informant role was revealed; arrested again January 1920. Although assured by Department of Justice agent J.F. Sawkin that he would be deported to Russia to allay suspicions and then be allowed to reenter the US, and his bail was paid by the Youngstown Sheet & Tool Company, he was arrested in Youngstown for operated an illegal alcohol still on March 26, 1920. Later claimed he was held in solitary confinement and “starved” for about two weeks to extract an incriminating confession. Spent more than a year in detention on Deer Island, and assaulted by other detainees for being an “agent provocateur” and placed in a separate cell for his own protection. Deported May 19, 1921 and not allowed to return.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Ed Burns
profiles.description:
Ed Burns was the assistant to W. E. Spear, the Seattle district secretary-treasurer of an IWW industrial union organization. On April 22, 1920, Seattle's police Red Squad raided the organization's office in the Globe Building, seized records said to include a directory of roughly twelve thousand members, and arrested Burns together with Spear and the office stenographer Alicia Rosenbaum. Contemporary reports said the prisoners were held incommunicado for investigation on open charges, and the defendants were brought toward trial in June 1920 under Washington's criminal-syndicalism and criminal-anarchy repression. Spear's case was dismissed on January 24, 1921 on the prosecution's motion; no verdict or dismissal notice specifically naming Burns has been located, so his disposition is unresolved.

He is not the Ed Burns of the Sacramento IWW case, who died in the Sacramento County Jail in November 1918 — seventeen months before the Globe Building raid — and who has his own record in this database.

profiles.name: Guglielmo Galeotti
profiles.description:
Guglielmo Galeotti was born 1871 in Santa Sofia, Italy. Immigrated to the United States in 1902.

Became an anarchist in Italy during the late 1880s and was regarded by Italian authorities as a dangerous subversive. Repeatedly arrested and imprisoned for subversive activities between 1888 and 1902. Fled briefly to Switzerland in 1901, but was expelled and arrested on unfounded suspicion of complicity in the assassination of King Umberto I. Subsequently emigrated to and then expelled from Trieste. After immigrating to the United States, lived in mining communities in Pennsylvania, Kansas, and Illinois and became a leading figure in the Kansas anarchist Gruppo 11 Novembre. In 1909 married fellow anarchist Alba Genisio. In 1911 joined other group members in traveling to Mexico to assist the anarchist Partido Liberal Mexicano during the Mexican Revolution but soon became disillusioned and returned to the United States. Deported on February 19, 1920. 

Although he remained under surveillance in Italy, authorities reported that by 1935 he had withdrawn from politics and allegedly showed sympathy toward the Fascist regime.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

Joined the South Slavic Branch of the Socialist Party of America in Pittsburgh and transferred into the Communist Party of America in 1919. Arrested in March 1920 and deported to Yugoslavia via Italy on June 22, 1920, during which all of his luggage was lost. 

Upon disembarkation in Naples, he was imprisoned for sixteen days due to misfiled paperwork from the Bureau of Immigration. He was then transported with bound hands to Trieste, and incarcerated in six different jails along the route. Writing from prison in Trieste on August 8, 1920, he stated: “The suffering was terrible. I am not able to write you everything about it. I do not think that human beings should be treated that way.”

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Mikhail Yakovlev
profiles.description:
Mikhail Yakovlev was born about 1899 in Vologda, Russia. Immigrated to the United States in 1916.

Born c. 1899, Vologda, Russia. Migrated to US in 1916 (jumped ship from the SS Czar). Sailor. Joined the Russian Branch of the IWW in New York City, of which he became secretary, as well as the Socialist Party and then the Second Russian Branch of the Communist Party. Arrested January 8, 1920. Declared: “I am a revolutionist…I believe in overthrowing all capitalistic forms of government…I have nothing against deportation to Russia. I love my motherland. I left my relatives there and I am quite willing to go there.” Deported January 22, 1921 on the SS Stockholm.

INS file 54860/597

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Napoleon Jones
profiles.description: Napoleon Jones is a US Navy veteran who recorded a police traffic stop in Sussex, Wisconsin, on May 4, 2025. Deputies subsequently stopped his vehicle, handcuffed him and took him to Waukesha County Jail. Reporting describes five hours in custody before release without citations or criminal charges. His federal civil-rights complaint alleges that the stop and arrest were retaliation for recording police. The complaint reproduces a sheriff's supervisor memorandum acknowledging that the traffic stop was unlawful and Jones could not be compelled to identify himself. Jones also alleges that deputies later used Flock license-plate searches to track his vehicle in retaliation for his complaint. Those retaliation claims are allegations in his civil lawsuit, not findings of a final judgment.

profiles.name: Nikolai Stechishin
profiles.description:
Nikolai Stechishin was born 1888.

Born 1888, Hlesczawa, Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, Austria-Hungary (present-day Ukraine). Ruthenian. Miner. Migrated to North America 1908 and became naturalized Canadian citizen. Migrated from Kaslo, British Columbia, to Spokane, Washington in 1913; returned Kaslo and migrated to Spokane again in 1916. Joined the IWW at an unknown date. Arrested in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, in March 1920 as part of local authorities’ “attempt to break up the I.W.W. element in the district”; indicted for criminal syndicalism. Deported to Canada September 28, 1920. However, in 1926 he managed to migrate to Alaska from Steward, British Columbia. Subsequent activities unknown.

INS 54325/36G

See also: Ancestry.com; The Spokesman-Review (Spokane WA), March 21 and 24, 1920

profiles.name: W. E. Spear
profiles.description: W. E. Spear was the Seattle district secretary-treasurer of an IWW industrial union organization. On April 22, 1920, Seattle's police Red Squad raided the organization's office in the Globe Building, seizing records said to include a directory of roughly twelve thousand members, and arrested Spear, his assistant Ed Burns, and the office stenographer Alicia Rosenbaum. Contemporary reports said the prisoners were held incommunicado for investigation on open charges. The defendants were brought toward trial in June 1920 under Washington's criminal-syndicalism and criminal-anarchy repression; the case against Spear was dismissed on January 24, 1921 on the prosecution's motion. No prison sentence is documented, and his actual pretrial custody span is uncertain because the records do not state whether or when he obtained bail. His full first and middle names are not established.
